knowledge: Treat Claude like a brilliant but new colleague: it has no context about you, your task, your customers or your organisation unless you give it.
A strong business prompt states the task, the background, who the output is for, why it matters, the format you want and any limits (length, tone, what to include or avoid).
Explaining the reason behind a request gives Claude your goal, so it can make better choices you did not spell out.
Examples are one of the most reliable ways to steer format, tone and structure. A few (about 3 to 5) varied, clearly labelled examples work better than one.
Even one sentence of role, such as "You are an HR adviser writing for new managers", focuses tone and perspective.
With long material, such as a contract or report, put the document first and your question at the end, and label each document clearly.
skills: Rewrite a vague one-line request into a prompt that names the goal, audience, format and constraints.
Apply the colleague test: would a co-worker with little context know exactly what to produce?
Add a template or a few examples when the output must match a house format or voice.
Ask directly for the depth you want ("give five options, each with pros and cons") instead of hoping Claude infers it.
examLens: Generic or off-target output usually means missing context. The best answer adds specifics (audience, purpose, format, policy), not emphasis.
When the output must match a set format or voice, the best answer supplies examples or a template.
Options that repeat the request louder (capitals, "IMPORTANT", "make it better") are distractors.
traps: Assuming Claude knows your company, policies, products or internal jargon.
Using fuzzy words like "brief", "professional" or "good" instead of concrete criteria such as a word count or required sections.
Giving a single example and getting near copies of it; use a few varied examples.

knowledge: Breaking a complex request into smaller steps is one of the first fixes Anthropic suggests when a prompt isn't giving a helpful answer.
Chaining means running a task as a sequence of steps, so you can inspect each intermediate result before it feeds the next step.
A common chain is draft, then review against clear criteria, then refine.
When order matters but you don't need to check in between, numbered steps inside one prompt are enough.
Each step should have one clear goal and a defined output. Errors caught early don't spread into later steps.
Planning the conversation up front, and batching simple related questions together, saves time and usage.
skills: Spot natural stages in a big request, such as gather facts, analyse, draft, then review.
Decide where a human check is needed between steps, especially before figures or claims are reused.
Choose between one prompt with numbered steps and a chain of separate turns.
Trace a wrong final result back to the step where it first appeared.
examLens: A request that bundles research, analysis and writing and returns shallow output: the answer is to split it into stages and review between them.
If the final output has a wrong fact, check the earliest step that produced it, not the final wording.
"Be more thorough" or "write more" added to the same giant prompt is a distractor.
traps: Asking for every deliverable in one message and expecting depth on each.
Splitting work into so many tiny steps that the overhead outweighs the benefit.
Skipping checks on intermediate outputs and hoping a final review catches everything.

knowledge: Treat Claude's first output as a draft: expect to review it and refine.
Before iterating, decide what "good" looks like (success criteria) and check each draft against it, using real examples of your work.
Useful feedback is specific: what is wrong, what to keep and what to change ("cut the intro to two sentences, keep the case study").
Change one thing at a time so you know which change helped or hurt.
Test a prompt on several varied real cases, not just one, before relying on it.
When a prompt works, save it as a reusable template or standing instruction so the result can be repeated.
skills: Write success criteria for a task before tweaking the prompt.

Run small, one-change experiments and compare the results.
Check a prompt across a varied sample and look for the pattern in the failures.
examLens: The best next step after a near-miss draft is targeted feedback in the same chat, not starting over or accepting it.
Iterating without criteria, or changing many things at once, is the realistic mistake to reject.
A prompt that worked on one example is not proven; test it on a varied set of real cases.
traps: Saying "try again" or "this is wrong" with no detail.
Changing role, examples, format and length all at once, then not knowing what caused the result.
Resending the same prompt in a new chat and hoping for a better draft.

knowledge: Analysis: give the data or document, the exact question and the criteria. For multi-step reasoning or detailed document analysis, thinking or a higher effort level helps.
Research: set clear success criteria and ask Claude to check claims across several sources. Web search suits simple current facts; Research suits in-depth, multi-source reports with citations.
Always review the sources Claude cites; the originals may hold context the summary left out.
Drafting: state the audience, purpose, key points, requirements and tone, and show an example of the voice you want.
Brainstorming: ask explicitly for many varied ideas, hold back judgement, then shortlist against criteria in a separate step.
Complex reasoning that needs no fresh web information calls for thinking or effort, not Research.
skills: Name the task type before writing the prompt and pick the matching strategy.
Separate idea generation from evaluation when brainstorming.
Choose between web search, Research and thinking based on whether you need current facts, many sources or deeper reasoning.
For analysis, ask Claude to show which figures or passages each conclusion rests on.
examLens: Match the strategy to the task: divergent (brainstorming) wants quantity and variety; convergent (analysis, drafting) wants criteria and constraints.
Sourced, in-depth briefings point to Research plus verification of the citations; a single current fact points to web search.
Distractors apply the wrong mode, such as fact-checking every brainstorm idea or brainstorming an analysis question.
traps: Using one generic prompt style for every kind of task.
Asking for "the best idea" when the goal is a wide set of options.
Relying on Claude's built-in knowledge for current events instead of web search with checked sources.

knowledge: Most weak outputs trace to a cause: generic means missing context; wrong format means format not stated; missed parts mean too many asks at once; wrong facts mean no source or no verification.
Claude can hallucinate: confident but wrong details, invented quotes, or confusion about current events. Don't treat it as a single source of truth.
Claude can also hallucinate its abilities, for example claiming it sent an email or created an external document. It cannot use tools that aren't connected.
To reduce invented details: let Claude say "I don't know", ask it to quote the passages it relies on, and limit it to the documents you provided. Then check.
If a chat has drifted across many topics, start a new conversation for the new topic.
Not every problem is a prompt problem. Some need a different feature or model, and work that needs a technical build should go to a Claude Developer or Architect.
skills: Describe the symptom precisely before changing anything.
Map the symptom to its most likely cause and apply the matching fix.
Recognise a claimed action that Claude could not actually have taken.
Spot when the fix is beyond prompting and escalate it.
examLens: "Most likely cause" questions reward the specific, checkable cause (missing context, too many asks, no source) over blaming the model.
If Claude claims it did something outside the chat with no connected tool, the answer is that it did not happen.
Needs like automatic overnight processing or system integration point to escalation, not more prompt tweaking.
traps: Trusting a confident tone as evidence of accuracy.
Switching models first, before checking what the prompt was missing.
Adding capital letters or repeating the instruction instead of fixing the cause.

knowledge: Feedback comes from your own review, from stakeholders ("too long", "too harsh") and from results, such as follow-up questions a template keeps causing.
Turn vague feedback into specific, testable instructions before regenerating.
Ask for concrete examples behind feedback so you can find the pattern rather than guess.
Feedback that keeps recurring belongs in standing instructions, such as a Project's instructions, so it applies every time. Context isn't shared between separate chats unless it is saved there.
If several rewordings haven't helped, change approach: add context or examples, decompose the task, use a different feature, or bring in an expert.
Keep human review where stakes are high, and fold the reviewer's recurring corrections back into the prompt.
skills: Translate a stakeholder's reaction into concrete prompt changes.
Test a revised prompt on a sample before rolling it out to everyone.
Recognise when it is time to stop rewording and change approach.
Record what worked so it can be reused.
examLens: The best response to feedback is specific, testable change, not "make it less harsh" or giving up on the task.
Recurring corrections point to standing instructions or a template, not repeated manual edits.
When repeated rewording fails, the answer changes the approach (examples, glossary, expert check).
traps: Passing vague feedback straight to Claude.
Rolling out a revised prompt without testing it.
Telling Claude a rule in one chat and expecting it in every other chat.
Dropping human review because the drafts have improved.

knowledge: Plan the conversation: give all the relevant context in one well-structured message and batch related questions together.
Keep reused documents and standing instructions in a Project instead of re-pasting them; reused project content also counts less against usage.
Start a new conversation for a new topic; long conversations, large attachments, tools and higher effort all use more of your allowance.
Match effort to the task: lower effort or no extended thinking for routine work, more for complex reasoning. A faster, lower-cost model suits simple, high-volume work.
Turn off web search and connectors you don't need for a task; tools use a lot of context.
Skills package a repeatable procedure so Claude applies it the same way whenever it's relevant. Efficiency never replaces checking what matters.

Choose the lightest setup that still meets the quality bar.
Build reusable templates for recurring outputs.
Keep verification steps when streamlining a workflow.

"Optimisations" that remove human checks on important facts are distractors.
traps: Using Research or maximum effort for everything "to be safe".
One endless chat for every topic.
Removing the review step because a template worked before.
